stories.title: Recommendations with a longer horizon
stories.summary: Exploring how Transformer models and reinforcement learning can connect financial goals, risk, and portfolio decisions.
stories.role: Simulation & architecture lead · collaborative graduate project
stories.contribution: Architected Transformer-based models and simulation-driven recommendation experiments within a collaborative graduate project; my assigned lead scope covers simulation, architecture, backtesting, and optimization.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: A useful allocation depends on when money is needed, what losses a person can tolerate, and whether a goal can actually be funded. Ranking assets by historical returns does not capture those constraints. This collaborative project explores personalized allocation as a goal-constrained decision problem, combining a product prototype with a separate research workflow.

sections.title: The product experience
sections.body: The application prototype collects goals, risk preferences, constraints, and existing holdings through a guided questionnaire, then presents allocations and simulated growth. The repository also includes portfolio profiles and an experimental public-official holdings browser. Its original web recommendation path uses a bounded ETF universe and weighted rules; the Transformer and reinforcement learning work lives in the research pipeline. The existence of both does not establish that the web app serves the research model.

sections.title: How the research system works
sections.body: Historical market series and company identity features feed a temporal Transformer that learns asset representations. A downstream Transformer combines representations with user context and generates a Gaussian allocation policy. Sampled weights run through a simulator with cash flows and goal withdrawals, and policy-gradient updates use the resulting reward. Cached representations reduce repeated upstream computation. The current RL worker uses a single Gaussian policy head; older research notes also describe dual-head variants.

sections.title: My role and collaboration
sections.body: The project plan identifies my role as simulation and architecture lead, responsible for repository structure, simulation, historical backtesting, and the optimization loop. Data/ML and financial logic have other named team leads. My resume and LinkedIn describe additional work across Transformer modeling, reinforcement learning, and evaluation. The system overview describes the collaborative project rather than assigning every module to one person.

sections.title: Evaluation and current limits
sections.body: The evaluation design uses historical holdouts, goal fulfillment, drawdown, volatility, and comparisons with S&P 500 and 60/40 allocations. Block-bootstrap scenarios broaden the sampled market paths, while chronological checks retain actual event ordering. The research notes have evolved alongside the code, so architecture descriptions here follow the reviewed worker implementation when the two differ. No independently verified outperformance result or production investment recommendation claim is available.

stories.evidence: Based on the local Financial_Analytics README, evolving RESEARCH_PLAN, reviewed temporal/RL worker code, and resume/LinkedIn descriptions. Team responsibilities follow the project plan. Tradeoffs reflect documented design history and consequences of the reviewed implementation; benchmark claims are intentionally omitted.

decisions.title: Learn market behavior before allocating
decisions.choice: Separate temporal asset representation learning from the user-conditioned allocation policy.
decisions.rationale: The research history describes a move from snapshot autoencoders toward sequence Transformers to represent order and changing market behavior. Reusing cached embeddings avoids retraining the representation model for every allocation experiment.
decisions.tradeoff: Training and cache management are more expensive than a simple scoring baseline. Frozen representations may omit signals the allocation objective would prefer; an adapter can reweight them but does not retrain the upstream model.

decisions.title: Optimize through the simulator
decisions.choice: Use a stochastic Gaussian policy and REINFORCE updates around a cash-flow and withdrawal simulator.
decisions.rationale: Discrete withdrawals and goal rules make the simulator non-differentiable. Policy gradients let sampled outcomes guide allocation without pretending that every simulator operation supports backpropagation.
decisions.tradeoff: Reward design and exploration noise materially affect convergence. Training costs more than a deterministic optimizer, and success in the simulator can reflect its assumptions rather than generalize to future markets.

decisions.title: Restrict historical features
decisions.choice: Classify features by temporal safety and exclude current market snapshots from historical embedding inputs.
decisions.rationale: Using today's valuation ratios when evaluating earlier years can introduce future information. The project instead emphasizes time-aligned derived signals and comparatively stable identity features.
decisions.tradeoff: Potentially useful fundamentals are excluded unless point-in-time history exists. Company classifications are not perfectly immutable either, so the feature registry reduces a leakage risk without proving every historical record is unbiased.

decisions.title: Resample market blocks
decisions.choice: Combine block-bootstrap simulations with chronological evaluation.
decisions.rationale: Resampling blocks diversifies the paths seen by the policy and reduces dependence on one exact sequence of crises and recoveries.
decisions.tradeoff: Block boundaries can break longer market cycles. Resampled scenarios complement held-out historical tests; they do not replace them or establish a forecast.

stories.title: Fog-Density Object Detection Research
stories.summary: Investigating density-aware object detection and adaptive feature gating in fog.
stories.contribution: Built a reproducible notebook workflow comparing RGB, predicted density, and predicted density with adaptive gating for YOLO11n, YOLO11m, and DETR.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: Camera-based object detection becomes less dependable when fog obscures visual detail. This study asks whether estimating fog density and conditioning the detector on that estimate can improve detection. It also tests whether suppressing selected fine spatial features helps. The current product is a reproducible research workflow for comparing hypotheses, rather than a driver-facing assistance application.

sections.title: The experimenter's workflow
sections.body: A researcher selects a setup, subset, or full profile; checks dataset coverage; trains or resumes a run; and exports comparisons without retraining. The project preserves the original density-feature notebook alongside the newer squint experiment namespace. This makes it possible to compare work over time without silently overwriting older outputs.

sections.title: How the study works
sections.body: A frozen fog-density estimator supplies a beta estimate to a shared adapter. YOLO11n, YOLO11m, and DETR are compared across RGB, predicted-density, and predicted-density-plus-squint arms. The squint intervention masks YOLO's P3 detector input or filters DETR spatial tokens while keeping positional information aligned. The research plan requires matched initialization, scene splits, seeds, and budgets so the comparison focuses on the intervention.

sections.title: Data and recovery
sections.body: The plan splits whole scenes to reduce train/test leakage and distinguishes Foggy Cityscapes beta labels from native nuScenes visibility. Projected nuScenes boxes are treated as a 2D evaluation proxy. Run identity includes configuration and input fingerprints; checkpoint handling is designed to preserve optimizer and RNG state and reject incompatible resumes. These controls make interrupted experiments more inspectable, although they are not evidence of detection quality.

sections.title: Evaluation and current limits
sections.body: The planned report includes mAP, AP50, recall, per-class and small-object performance, density estimation error, seed spread, and end-to-end mean/p95 latency. The estimator and gate overhead belong in timing. Positive, null, and negative outcomes are all meaningful. No completed matched-run evidence has been reviewed here that establishes accuracy gains, compute savings, or readiness for use in a vehicle.

decisions.title: Three matched comparison arms
decisions.choice: Keep RGB and predicted-density controls alongside an independently trained squint arm.
decisions.rationale: A density adapter and a gate change different things. Keeping both controls helps determine whether any measured difference comes from adding density information or from feature suppression.
decisions.tradeoff: The experiment matrix is larger and consumes more training time. Using only one baseline would be cheaper but would leave the source of an improvement ambiguous.

decisions.title: Adapt the gate to each architecture
decisions.choice: Mask YOLO P3 features and filter DETR spatial tokens instead of forcing identical mechanics onto both models.
decisions.rationale: The reviewed plan recognizes that the YOLO detection pyramid and the configured DETR spatial representation have different contracts.
decisions.tradeoff: The interventions are not identical, so cross-model results need careful interpretation. Zeroing YOLO features does not skip their computation, and DETR filtering can damage small-object recall or positional alignment.

decisions.title: Predict density at evaluation time
decisions.choice: Use a frozen density estimator and report its errors and overhead.
decisions.rationale: A practical experiment should not rely on perfect fog labels that would be unavailable for a new image. Freezing the predictor also helps isolate detector changes.
decisions.tradeoff: The detector inherits prediction error, and the estimator adds latency. Oracle-density results, when possible, answer a different question and need separate labeling.

decisions.title: Favor reproducible recovery
decisions.choice: Version outputs and identify checkpoints by configuration, data, and arm.
decisions.rationale: Long experiments can be interrupted. Explicit identities reduce the chance that a resume silently combines incompatible runs.
decisions.tradeoff: More metadata, validation, and storage are required. Faster ad hoc iteration is sacrificed for comparisons that can be traced and repeated.

stories.title: Trajectory — Financial Planning
stories.summary: Retirement trajectory tooling connecting spending, saving, and investing decisions with financial timelines.
stories.contribution: Built retirement and loan calculation modules, financial projections, and shareable URL-based planning profiles.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: Budgets usually explain where money went. Trajectory explores a different question: how today's spending, contributions, and goals change the time needed to reach financial independence. The product connects immediate cash-flow decisions with a longer retirement trajectory, while making room for manual inputs and optional connected account data.

sections.title: The product experience
sections.body: Users configure a financial profile, inspect projections, and adjust income, expenses, contributions, property assumptions, and goals. A CSV import path and optional Plaid account connections reduce repeated data entry. Shareable profiles and backup/import workflows support portability. More recent development focuses on retaining edits, focused editors, reserve goals, and making uncertain connected data visible before it replaces manual values.

sections.title: How the application works
sections.body: The reviewed codebase separates pure calculation engines, application services, browser controllers, and thin Plaid HTTP handlers. The profile codec versions a compact representation for URL transport. Current work also adds local persistence and recovery controls. An architecture document proposes a broader canonical plan model and repository boundary; that target design is not described here as a completed migration.

sections.title: Reliability as product behavior
sections.body: Losing a plan or silently substituting a bad balance would undermine the product more than a missing chart. Development notes record fixes for startup hydration overwriting restored values, storage failures, cross-tab conflicts, incomplete provider pagination, and negative or unknown balances. The revised flows retain manual values when connected data needs review, preserve prior records during writes, and expose backup and recovery options.

sections.title: Validation and current limits
sections.body: The October 18 source notes report a 98-case desktop/mobile browser pass alongside unit and synthetic local-production checks. A subsequent hands-on review still identified UX gaps, including inline scrolling, long editors, and a reserve-source mismatch. Those results are historical evidence from the project, not tests rerun for this portfolio. The personal release remains a preview; financial accuracy, provider reconciliation, performance gates, and release rehearsal are not established as complete.

decisions.title: Translate finances into time
decisions.choice: Center the experience on retirement trajectory and the effects of changing assumptions.
decisions.rationale: This connects individual spending and saving decisions with a goal users can understand, rather than making transaction categories the only product output.
decisions.tradeoff: A clear timeline can look more certain than its inputs warrant. Assumptions and data confidence need to remain visible, and a compelling chart is not proof of calculation accuracy.

decisions.title: Keep calculations separate from screens
decisions.choice: Use pure calculation modules and service boundaries, with architecture checks on dependencies.
decisions.rationale: Financial behavior is easier to test when it can run without a browser or provider. A shared calculation path also reduces differences between onboarding and dashboard views.
decisions.tradeoff: The current mutable profile and controller refresh flow still create coupling. The documented canonical-plan architecture requires further migration rather than being solved by folder names alone.

decisions.title: Offer portable plans
decisions.choice: Support versioned profile URLs, local persistence, and explicit backups.
decisions.rationale: These paths let users revisit and move a plan without requiring a hosted account system for every experiment.
decisions.tradeoff: Encoded URLs are not encryption and may expose included plan data when shared. Local storage and backups also require versioning, validation, and clear handling when writes fail.

decisions.title: Bound connected-data work
decisions.choice: Use limited provider concurrency and pagination, preserve manual values on questionable balances, and separate bank access from profile links.
decisions.rationale: This reduces the chance that partial or malformed account data is treated as a complete financial picture.
decisions.tradeoff: A failed or bounded refresh can leave information incomplete. The UI must distinguish stale, missing, and reviewed data, and historical test passes do not prove every live account is reconciled.

stories.title: MTG Vault — Collection Tracker
stories.summary: A desktop and mobile card collection tracker designed for rapid cataloging.
stories.contribution: Built keyboard-driven card entry with set, printing, finish, condition, and language selection.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: Cataloging a physical card collection is repetitive work. A collector needs to distinguish sets, printings, finishes, condition, and language, often for thousands of cards. A complete database form is not necessarily a fast capture experience. MTG Vault starts with the entry loop, then adds browsing, valuation estimates, and portability around it.

sections.title: The collector's workflow
sections.body: A collector types a card name, chooses a set and printing with the keyboard, selects finish and condition, and presses Enter. They can immediately begin the next card. Existing matching variants increase in quantity rather than becoming duplicate rows. Browsing adds search, sorting, details, and collection statistics, while mobile uses a dedicated navigation and selection layout.

sections.title: How the system works
sections.body: Scryfall supplies card identity, images, printing metadata, and reference prices. A variant identity combines the card, set, style, finish, condition, and language. Storage interfaces support Google Sheets through CSV reads and Apps Script writes, plus a local CSV representation in browser storage. A sync queue merges matching operations and sends batches rather than a separate request for each keystroke.

sections.title: Portability and recovery
sections.body: CSV import detects common collection formats, normalizes aliases, resolves printings, and previews results with found, unfound, and error counts. Export targets include collector and marketplace workflows. For remote write failures, the documented recovery paths include an unsynced CSV backup and switching to local storage. Shared collection mode is read-only; it is a separate experience from editing an owned collection.

sections.title: Validation and current limits
sections.body: The repository includes tests for card identity, CSV parsing, import behavior, collection actions, sync queues, and Moxfield handling. The product document distinguishes intended behavior from remaining implementation gaps. Price fields are market references, not realizable sale prices, and remote storage depends on the user's sheet and Apps Script setup. No measured entry-speed advantage, large-scale multi-user guarantee, or commerce capability is claimed.

decisions.title: Optimize for repeated capture
decisions.choice: Use a keyboard-first sequence of small choices, with a separate mobile layout.
decisions.rationale: The product document identifies repetitive physical-card logging as the primary job. Keeping the collector in one selection loop avoids repeated mouse-driven forms.
decisions.tradeoff: Keyboard controls need discoverability and focus discipline. Mobile cannot simply inherit the desktop layout, so it adds interaction and accessibility work.

decisions.title: Preserve variant identity
decisions.choice: Match on printing attributes, finish, condition, and language instead of card name alone.
decisions.rationale: Two copies with the same name can be materially different collection records. A composite identity lets true duplicates aggregate while distinct variants remain separate.
decisions.tradeoff: Imports and edits become more complex because external tools name styles and finishes differently. Incorrect normalization can still split or merge records.

decisions.title: Use portable storage adapters
decisions.choice: Support Sheets/Apps Script and a local CSV storage implementation.
decisions.rationale: This fits a collector-owned dataset that remains inspectable and exportable without a dedicated hosted account backend.
decisions.tradeoff: Sheets setup and service limits become product constraints. Local storage depends on the browser, and this approach does not establish the transaction or collaboration guarantees of a purpose-built database.

decisions.title: Batch rapid changes
decisions.choice: Merge matching queued operations and send debounced batches.
decisions.rationale: Fast entry creates bursts of small changes. Combining them reduces request overhead and keeps the interaction from waiting on every remote write.
decisions.tradeoff: The visible collection and remote sheet can temporarily differ. Failure recovery and unsynced backups matter, and batching alone does not prove conflict-safe concurrent editing.

stories.title: Wordrix — Vocabulary Learning
stories.summary: An ML-powered vocabulary game using semantic similarity to help people learn foreign words.
stories.contribution: Built a context-based word embedding model and neural similarity engine for real-time semantic hints.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: Vocabulary practice can become a memorization exercise disconnected from how words relate. Wordrix explores an interactive alternative: use semantic similarity as a hint so a learner can reason about neighboring concepts while learning foreign words. The product joins a small language-modeling experiment with a web game.

sections.title: The learning experience
sections.body: A learner receives semantic feedback rather than only a correct/incorrect signal. The model represents words in a reduced-dimensional context space and uses a neural similarity calculation to produce hints. The historical project summary describes an interactive game connecting foreign and English vocabulary; detailed current screen behavior and language coverage have not been verified.

sections.title: The data and model workflow
sections.body: The resume describes crawling roughly 10,000 Wikipedia pages and cleaning about 50,000 entries. Preparation included stop-word removal, minimum context filtering, and topic-focused sentences, including animals and fruits. Training-data variants and within-group similarity-score distributions were compared to inspect model behavior. The application work spans an AngularJS interface and Java backend.

sections.title: What the project demonstrates
sections.body: The interesting engineering work is the connection between data preparation, representation quality, and feedback a learner can interpret. A mathematically valid similarity score may still be a poor game hint if too many unrelated words score closely or a topic is underrepresented. That makes examining the score distribution part of the product design, not just an offline model task.

sections.title: Evidence and current limits
sections.body: Available evidence is the historical resume material, not a newly reviewed local repository or a live service audit. It supports the pipeline, implementation scope, and evaluation approach but does not establish learning outcomes, current uptime, multilingual accuracy, or comparison with modern language models. The original demo address is omitted because availability has not been verified.

decisions.title: Use context-based word representations
decisions.choice: Represent words with embeddings and calculate similarity for game feedback.
decisions.rationale: Context-based representations provide a way to rank related concepts rather than treating every vocabulary guess as an exact string match. This is an engineering interpretation of the described implementation; the original decision log is unavailable.
decisions.tradeoff: Similarity reflects the training corpus and is not the same as translation correctness. Sparse words and differences between languages can produce misleading hints.

decisions.title: Filter training contexts
decisions.choice: Clean crawled text and focus parts of the dataset on identifiable topics.
decisions.rationale: The source describes stop-word removal and meaningful-context filtering. These steps aim to make the learned relationships more useful for the intended vocabulary groups.
decisions.tradeoff: Filtering removes noise but also reduces coverage and can amplify topic bias. A clean animal vocabulary subset does not imply equal quality for other subjects.

decisions.title: Inspect score behavior before game claims
decisions.choice: Compare training variants and the spread of similarity scores within word groups.
decisions.rationale: A usable hint system needs distinctions a learner can act on. The resume records this distribution-based inspection rather than an unsupported claim of user learning gains.
decisions.tradeoff: Offline scores do not measure retention, fairness across languages, or whether users understand the hint. A learner study would be needed to establish those outcomes.

stories.title: Tsao Wang Family Foundation Website
stories.summary: A nonprofit website designed for ease of use and maintenance by nontechnical administrators.
stories.contribution: Led collaboration with a developer and UX contributor to design the nonprofit website.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: A nonprofit needs to keep resources and messages current without making every edit a developer task. The foundation website prioritizes a content workflow that nontechnical administrators can operate, along with clear resource navigation for English and Traditional Chinese readers.

sections.title: The editor and visitor experience
sections.body: An administrator edits text, image links, and resource records in a Google Spreadsheet. The website reads the published sheet data when visitors load the page and maps it into reusable sections. Visitors browse foundation information and resource categories with language-specific content. This puts routine publishing into a familiar editing tool while keeping the public interface separate.

sections.title: How the website works
sections.body: The reviewed project uses React and Vite, reusable page and section components, a custom CSS-variable design system, and PapaParse for published CSV data. Fetch functions load resources and messages, parse column headers, and convert rows into page content. Language-specific sheet data supplies translated content rather than automatically translating a single source.

sections.title: My contribution and delivery
sections.body: LinkedIn describes leading collaboration with a developer and a UX contributor. The local code and README support the component-based site and spreadsheet content architecture, while the changelog records work on responsive navigation, consistent page layout, branding, metadata, and dropdown behavior. These describe the team's implementation; they do not attribute every code change to me personally.

sections.title: Maintenance and current limits
sections.body: The README documents a static-hosted deployment and a nontechnical content guide. The older resume and local README reference different hosting addresses; the portfolio keeps the previously supplied site link without asserting a newly verified migration. The reviewed fetch functions log failures, so a rich editor preview or robust public fallback should not be assumed. Language parity, accessibility conformance, and availability are not independently certified here.

decisions.title: Use Sheets as the content source
decisions.choice: Read published CSV content from a spreadsheet rather than requiring an administrative CMS application.
decisions.rationale: The project explicitly aims for maintenance without technical expertise. Editors can update familiar rows while the React site owns presentation.
decisions.tradeoff: Spreadsheet columns become an implicit content contract. Renamed headers, malformed links, or a publishing change can affect the site, and a published sheet is appropriate for public content only.

decisions.title: Keep a custom visual system
decisions.choice: Use CSS variables and reusable React sections instead of a large styling framework.
decisions.rationale: The README documents a lightweight, consistent design system and shared layout components. Repeated resource pages can share spacing and presentation rules.
decisions.tradeoff: Custom navigation, responsive behavior, and accessibility need to be maintained directly. A small dependency footprint does not by itself prove a faster or more accessible site.

decisions.title: Maintain explicit translated content
decisions.choice: Use English and Traditional Chinese content sheets.
decisions.rationale: Separate translations let editors control the wording and context readers see, rather than depending on an automatic translation step.
decisions.tradeoff: Two versions can drift and need editorial coordination. This architecture provides language support without guaranteeing translation completeness or parity.

stories.title: Personal Portfolio
stories.summary: A server-rendered portfolio presenting engineering experience and applied ML work.
stories.role: Product design, content architecture & full-stack engineering
stories.contribution: Built a recruiter-oriented portfolio with server-rendered pages, a validated content service, and a path from concise accomplishments to detailed project case studies.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: A resume can list experience but has limited room to explain judgment. This portfolio gives recruiters a quick way to assess technical fit, then lets engineers and collaborators inspect the product problem, implementation, evidence, and tradeoffs behind each project. The challenge is making the deeper material easy to reach without turning the homepage into a long technical report.

sections.title: The visitor's path
sections.body: The homepage presents positioning, selected work, career history, and contact. The expanded resume supplies accomplishments and project summaries. Each project links to a dedicated case study, and a project directory offers a complete browsing path. Case studies include the user problem, workflow, system overview, contribution, current limits, and structured design choices.

sections.title: How content reaches the page
sections.body: A Python/FastAPI service loads a JSON content file, validates it with Pydantic, filters unpublished stories, and calculates a content revision. Next.js fetches that content on the server and validates the response with Zod before rendering. Pages, metadata, and the sitemap derive from the same published story collection. Production uses Vercel's internal service binding; the backend has no public API ingress.

sections.title: Designing for assessment
sections.body: The visual system uses restrained typography, readable prose, semantic headings, and clear links. A simplified flow diagram supports the explanation when useful. The homepage stays curated while the project directory grows. Tradeoff cards separate the actual choice, the reason it fits, and the cost or limitation, so a technical reader can inspect judgment without decoding a wall of stack names.

sections.title: Verification and current limits
sections.body: Existing checks cover API contracts, invalid content, draft exclusion, recovery, concurrent reads, accessibility, narrow screens, navigation without JavaScript, and a JavaScript transfer budget. The resume adds print-specific behavior. These automated and local checks support the reviewed release paths; they do not establish recruiter conversion, field performance, or search ranking. The new project pages are local changes until deployed.

decisions.title: Keep the homepage curated
decisions.choice: Use a few selected stories on the homepage and a dedicated directory for all personal projects.
decisions.rationale: The visitor can get an initial view quickly, then deliberately choose a deeper project or the full resume.
decisions.tradeoff: Some projects require another click to discover. Explicit directory and resume links are needed so curation does not make the rest of the work invisible.

decisions.title: Validate one content source twice
decisions.choice: Use JSON/Pydantic at the content boundary and Zod at the server-rendering boundary.
decisions.rationale: Content needs stable shapes across Python and TypeScript. Validation catches malformed data before pages silently display partial or invented information.
decisions.tradeoff: Two contract definitions must remain aligned, and schema extensions need compatibility checks. A simpler repository could import static content directly and avoid this service boundary.

decisions.title: Render with an internal content service
decisions.choice: Fetch content on the server through a deployment service binding and render HTML for visitors.
decisions.rationale: This fits the Python/React stack and keeps the content API internal while allowing ordinary links and meaningful HTML without client-side data fetching.
decisions.tradeoff: A backend outage can affect page rendering. Compared with a wholly static export, this adds runtime availability, service configuration, and operational checks.

decisions.title: Use conceptual diagrams and scoped evidence
decisions.choice: Show a simplified workflow and pair it with implementation status, source scope, and limits.
decisions.rationale: A diagram helps explain the system while source notes distinguish reviewed code, historical descriptions, and proposed work.
decisions.tradeoff: A simplified view omits operational detail, and some older projects have thinner evidence. The page needs enough prose to avoid presenting a conceptual flow as a complete deployment architecture.
